Note::for_each_flat¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signature¶

template<class Fn>
  requires std::invocable<Fn&, std::string_view>
void Note::for_each_flat(Fn&& fn) const

Visit Every Text Or Byte Cell¶

for_each_flat() invokes fn(cell) once for each Text or Bytes cell. The argument is a borrowed std::string_view; no cell string is allocated or decoded. Use the method when a callback expresses the work more directly than an explicit iterator loop: accumulating metrics, feeding a parser, writing to a stream, hashing cells, or copying into an external representation.

Traversal is flat and row-major for every rank. A scalar invokes the callback once. A defined empty Note invokes it zero times. The method rejects an undefined handle and native Bool, Int64, and Float64 Notes before invoking the callback at all.

The callable may capture state and may return any value; return values are discarded. If it throws, traversal stops immediately and the same exception propagates to the caller. Effects already performed by earlier invocations are not rolled back. That behavior makes early termination possible, but callers must provide their own transactional boundary when partial external writes would be unsafe.

for_each_flat() itself allocates nothing and performs one indirect callable invocation per cell. A direct range-based loop can be preferable in a very hot path when the compiler can inline the loop body more clearly; both traverse the same packed arena and have O(numel()) time.

Example 1: Aggregate Without Materializing A Vector¶

const auto grid = pluss::note::make(
    std::vector<std::string>{"r0c0", "r0c1", "r0c2", "r1c0", "r1c1", "r1c2"},
    std::array<std::int64_t, 2>{2, 3});
std::size_t cells = 0;
std::size_t bytes = 0;
grid.for_each_flat([&](std::string_view cell) {
  ++cells;
  bytes += cell.size();
});
std::cout << "cells=" << cells << " bytes=" << bytes << '\n';

Output¶

cells=6 bytes=24

The callback sees six cells, not two row Notes.

Example 2: Stream Cells In Logical Order¶

const auto words = pluss::note::make({"north", "east", "south", "west"});
bool first = true;
words.for_each_flat([&](std::string_view word) {
  std::cout << (first ? "" : " | ") << word;
  first = false;
});
std::cout << '\n';

Output¶

north | east | south | west

Example 3: Stop By Throwing¶

const auto words = pluss::note::make({"north", "east", "south", "west"});
try {
  words.for_each_flat([](std::string_view cell) {
    if (cell == "south") throw std::runtime_error("stop at south");
  });
} catch (const std::runtime_error& error) {
  std::cout << "callback error=" << error.what() << '\n';
}

Output¶

callback error=stop at south

This is exception propagation, not a hidden boolean-break protocol. Use an explicit iterator loop when ordinary break is clearer.

Example 4: Empty Notes Make No Calls¶

const auto empty = pluss::note::make(std::vector<std::string>{});
std::size_t calls = 0;
empty.for_each_flat([&](std::string_view) { ++calls; });
std::cout << "empty calls=" << calls << '\n';

Output¶

empty calls=0

Example 5: Undefined Is Not A Defined Empty Note¶

try {
  pluss::Note::undefined().for_each_flat([](std::string_view) {});
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "undefined callback: rejected\n";
}

Output¶

undefined callback: rejected

Example 6: Traverse Native Values Natively¶

const auto values = pluss::note::make(std::vector<std::int64_t>{3, 1, 4});
std::cout << "integers=";
for (const auto value : values.integers()) std::cout << value << ' ';
std::cout << '\n';

Output¶

integers=3 1 4

Using integers() avoids both textual formatting and variant dispatch.
